nominee.t: Confirmed Republican nominee: won the May 19, 2026 GOP primary with 421,754 votes (85.4%) over Ken McFeeters (9.6%) and Will Santivasci (5.0%); no runoff needed.

ballot.t: General-election ballot lists only Tuberville (R) and Doug Jones (D) plus a write-in line; no independent or third-party candidate for governor appears in Politics1, the Alabama Reflector voter guide or Wikipedia's ballot table. Independents had until May 19, 2026 to file 42,458 signatures. The Secretary of State's certified candidate list itself was not retrieved.

oneliner.t: Republican U.S. senator from Alabama since January 2021 and former college football head coach (Ole Miss, Auburn, Texas Tech, Cincinnati), Trump-endorsed nominee for governor whose eligibility under the seven-year residency rule is being challenged in court.

born.t: September 18, 1954, Camden, Arkansas (Wikipedia; Senate bio does not state birthplace — single secondary source)

hometown.t: Camden, Arkansas (raised there; Harmony Grove High School, 1972)

profile.residence: Auburn, AL (claimed; also owns a home in Santa Rosa Beach, FL — residency disputed in pending litigation)

upbringing.t: Tuberville grew up in Camden, Arkansas, one of three children of Olive Nell (Chambliss) and Charles R. Tuberville Jr.; his Senate biography says his father was a World War II veteran awarded five Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart. He graduated from Harmony Grove High School in 1972 and earned a physical-education degree from Southern State College (now Southern Arkansas University) in 1976. He then spent about four decades in college coaching, including assistant jobs at Miami and Texas A&M before head-coaching jobs in Mississippi, Alabama, Texas and Ohio.

education.school: Southern State College (now Southern Arkansas University)

career.role: Co-founder/partner name on hedge fund later found to have defrauded investors (he was not charged)
career.org: TS Capital Management / TS Capital Partners

platform.t: Eliminate the state grocery tax, 'cut taxes even further', and 'audit every state dollar'; pitches 'less taxes, more results'.
Protect school choice and the CHOOSE Act education savings accounts; reward good teachers and hold poor ones accountable; workforce focus.
Says he will send the National Guard into Montgomery (which he calls a 'war zone'), Birmingham and Mobile on day one.

Supports data-center growth but says they must 'pay full taxes' at the highest property-tax rate, get no tax breaks or abatements, pay for their own power, avoid fresh drinking water for cooling, and that communities get 'the final say'; opposes a moratorium.
Opposes the Affordable Care Act (under which Medicaid expansion is offered) and has supported individual health savings accounts.
Launch themes: oppose 'woke ideology', create jobs, improve education, border security.

promises.t: Send the National Guard into Montgomery, Birmingham and Mobile 'on Day One'.
End tax breaks for data centers, tax them at the maximum property-tax rate, and let communities decide where they are built.
'I will protect Alabamians from paying a single cent more for their energy' (data centers).
Protect the CHOOSE Act school-choice program.

claims.claim: "My wife and I, Suzanne, moved here over 25 years ago."

record.t: He became Auburn's head coach in 1999, so he first moved to Alabama more than 25 years before 2025. But the record shows long periods elsewhere: head coach at Texas Tech (2010–12) and Cincinnati (2013–16); in a 2017 ESPN video he said he had retired to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida; his Florida beach home got a Florida homestead exemption in 2018; he voted in Florida in November 2018 and registered to vote in Alabama on March 28, 2019.

claims.claim: "I live in Auburn." (also the residence stated on his Senate biography)

said.where: remarks reported by 1819 News; Senate 'About' page

record.t: Disputed and in litigation. The Auburn (Cherry Street) house has carried an Alabama homestead exemption since 2018, but property records showed it owned by his wife and son until he was added to the deed on May 7, 2024. A 2023 Washington Post analysis cited campaign-finance and property records pointing to the Santa Rosa Beach, Florida, home. He has said he spends 'a few days a month' in Destin, Florida. No court has ruled on the facts: a quo warranto suit was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (July 9, 2026) and the appeal was fully briefed at the Alabama Supreme Court as of Sept. 4, 2026.

claims.claim: "Unlike Doug Jones, Coach has also accepted ZERO PAC (political action committee) money."

said.where: campaign manager Jordan Doufexis statement to Alabama Reflector

record.t: The same Alabama Reflector review of his state filings found about $10,000 in PAC contributions (Diversified Gas & Oil PAC $2,500; Travelers PAC $2,500; Home Depot PAC $5,000) plus in-kind PAC contributions (BANKPAC $3,600; Truk PAC $7,200; Alabama Farm PAC nearly $3,000). His campaign has said it returns PAC checks; the filings reviewed still show the contributions above.

claims.claim: He "helped pass the largest working-class tax cuts in history" (One Big Beautiful Bill Act).

said.where: first TV ad ('Less taxes, more results')

record.t: There is no standard measure of a 'working-class' tax cut. PolitiFact found the 2025 law is not the largest tax cut in U.S. history as a share of GDP (third since 1980 counting the extended 2017 cuts; tied for seventh counting only new cuts) and noted some lower-income families may pay more because enhanced ACA premium credits were not extended. His Yea vote on the law is covered in the separate key-votes file.

claims.claim: He "delivered Alabama's biggest tax refund ever."

record.t: No Alabama-specific refund total was found. Yellowhammer News noted only a national Treasury figure (average refund above $3,400, up 11%). Federal refunds also are not delivered by one senator.

claims.claim: Delivered "over $2,800 in annual savings" on taxes for Alabama.

said.where: first TV ad (as described by ADN)

record.t: The ad's source for $2,800 was not found. Sen. Katie Britt's 2025 op-ed on the same law used a different figure (an average $2,200 tax increase avoided) and gave no source.

claims.claim: Opponents' education plan "kicks tens of thousands of children out of the school of their choice."

record.t: More than 34,000 students were approved for CHOOSE Act accounts for 2026–27, so 'tens of thousands' matches program size. But Jones said on July 29–30, 2026: 'The kids that are in there now, let them finish, but quit taking applications.' He later vowed to 'stop the CHOOSE Act in its tracks' without saying current students would lose funding.

claims.claim: Montgomery is a "war zone"; Mobile and Birmingham are "dangerous."

said.where: TV ad on crime (released the Tuesday before Oct. 1)

record.t: Characterization, not a checkable figure; the visible reporting cited no crime statistics from the ad.

claims.short: Five SEC West titles, one SEC crown

said.where: Senate office 'About Coach' bio page (tuberville.senate.gov/about), used as his own published bio because the campaign bio page coachforgovernor.com and its web.archive.org copy could not be opened (accessed 2026-10-08)

record.t: He was Auburn's head coach for the 1999 through 2008 seasons, which is 10 seasons (85–40). The '11 years' figure only works if late 1998, when he was hired, is counted as a year.

claims.claim: Retired after the 2016 season and then joined ESPN's broadcast staff.

said.where: Senate office 'About Coach' bio page (tuberville.senate.gov/about), used as his own published bio because the campaign bio page coachforgovernor.com and its web.archive.org copy could not be opened (accessed 2026-10-08)

record.t: His last head-coaching job was Cincinnati (2013–2016), and he was an ESPN college-football color analyst in 2017. The page's further details (full-time role, partnered with Mike Patrick, 'top 50 winningest coaches') were not confirmed in the sources opened, so they are not part of this rating.

said.t: Campaign: Tuberville has accepted 'ZERO PAC money' and does 'not solicit or accept PAC contributions'.

did.t: State filings show cash and in-kind PAC contributions earlier in the race and $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC in September 2026.

said.t: Called a congressional stock-trading ban 'ridiculous'; in 2024 said 'I don't do it myself, I've got people that do it.'

did.t: Continued trading through advisers: 1,356 trades per Quiver Quantitative as of Oct. 2025; about $7.16 million in 2024 trade volume per ADN.

said.t: Campaign said he had accepted zero PAC money.

did.t: Took $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC, per state filings reported in September.

entries.t: Strong support; said opposition was fueled by Chinese social-media influence and answered the claim that data centers ruin the climate with 'bull crap'.
Data centers should 'pay full taxes' and the full cost of their energy; communities get 'the final say'; end incentives and abatements.
'Tax breaks, no more' ad; cosponsored the federal Ratepayer Protection Act.
His Senate committee took PAC money: $777,079 from other committees in 2019–20, $232,850 in 2021–22, $324,300 in 2023–24.
Governor campaign says it does not accept PAC money; filings show about $10,000 cash plus in-kind PAC money through July, then $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC in September.
Warned that 'picking sides in the Middle East… could get really messy'; days later said 'We stand with Israel' and he was '120% behind Israel', calling for Hamas to be 'totally wiped out'.
Called Biden's support for a ban a 'dig' at Nancy Pelosi; defended trading through advisers.

pac_note.t: Itemized PAC money reported by news outlets: Diversified Gas & Oil PAC $2,500, Travelers PAC $2,500, Home Depot PAC $5,000 (cash), in-kind BANKPAC $3,600, Truk PAC $7,200, Alabama Farm PAC ~$3,000 (through July 2026); none in August; Alabama Realtors PAC $100,000 (September). Over 90% of first-day money came in contributions of $20,000+. Corporations may give directly under Alabama law; reported corporate checks include NaphCare $100,000, VGW Luckyland $100,000, Applied Digital $25,000, CVS $20,000, AT&T $15,000, CSX $5,000.

superpac_donors.pac: Club for Growth Action (2020 Senate race; amount spent per Club for Growth)

money_history.office: U.S. Senate (Tuberville for Senate, Inc. C00701672; candidate S0AL00230)

corp.t: Business and trade-group PAC money in his federal career: e.g., Nucor, Raytheon Technologies, FedEx, Boeing, U.S. Steel, Vulcan Materials, Marathon Petroleum, Home Depot and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama PACs ($5,000 each, 2020 cycle); Cadence Bank, Regions, Endo Pharmaceuticals and many agriculture trade PACs (2024 cycle). In the governor's race, direct corporate contributions (NaphCare $100,000; VGW Luckyland $100,000; Applied Digital $25,000; CVS $20,000; AT&T $15,000; CSX $5,000) and $100,000 from the Alabama Realtors PAC. In 2020, the Club for Growth Action super PAC spent $1,433,763 for him; its own donors were not retrieved.

lobby.t: Track AIPAC counts $29,184 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs and their large donors (lists AIPAC, AMP, RJC, USI); FEC-itemized U.S. Israel PAC gifts of $500 (2020) and $4,000 (2024). No UDP or other pro-Israel super PAC spending found.

overlap.asset: About 130 stock and option trades Jan–May 2021, including health-care companies
Wheat, corn, soybean and cattle futures (multiple trades, June–July 2023)

Sold stakes in IBM, Honeywell and Accenture, which the Alabama Political Reporter grouped among defense contractors (no per-stock amounts given). Separately reported to have held up to $50,000 of Lockheed Martin during a Sept. 2023 hearing featuring Lockheed's CEO

note.t: Senate eFD index (secondary copy) shows annual reports for CY2021–CY2025 filed in August of the following year, with extensions listed for the 2022–2025 reports, and many periodic transaction reports through July 2026. His 2020 annual report listed jointly held Santa Rosa Beach, FL condominiums, a 2012 Bank of America mortgage, an Alabama Retirement Systems pension and WB Studio royalties. A New York Times analysis cited by ADN called his agriculture-contract trades 'possible conflicts.' The 2021 trades included an Alibaba put-option sale ($15,001–$50,000). Net worth was not computed because the primary eFD could not be opened.

committees: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (Education and the American Family Subcommittee chair)

law_note.t: Per his office's releases: Supporting Families of the Fallen Act (Oct 2022), GI Bill dependents fix S. 3606 (Dec 27, 2022), Restoring Benefits to Defrauded Veterans Act (118th Congress). Not verified on congress.gov (blocked).

democracy.t: After the 2020 election, likened results to referees adding touchdowns after a game ended — AP described this as backing Trump's unsupported fraud claim.
As senator-elect signaled he would join an objection to the Electoral College count ('You'll see what's coming'); Trump called him a 'hero'.
One of six senators who voted to sustain the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (failed 6–93).
One of seven senators who voted to sustain the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (failed).
Voted against creating an independent commission on the Jan. 6 attack; told ABC News in 2025 he fully supported Trump's Jan. 6 pardons.
Told Steve Bannon that Democrats 'stole the election from President Trump' in 2020.
Said on Newsmax 'we probably have four or five senators that didn't legally win', offering no evidence or names.

note.t: Born and raised in Arkansas. Lived in Alabama as Auburn's coach (1999–2008); coached in Texas and Ohio 2010–2016; said in 2017 he had retired to Santa Rosa Beach, FL, and voted in Florida in Nov. 2018; registered to vote in Alabama March 28, 2019. Whether he has been an Alabama resident since Nov. 2019 (the seven-year test) is the subject of a pending Alabama Supreme Court appeal, so a year count is not given.

eligibility_challenge.t: Two veterans (Brooke Lynn Dorgan and Justin Jude LeBlanc) filed a quo warranto suit claiming he does not meet the Alabama Constitution's seven-year residency requirement for governor. Montgomery Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed it July 9, 2026 for lack of jurisdiction, without ruling on the facts. Plaintiffs appealed July 14. Tuberville, AG Steve Marshall and the Alabama GOP asked the court to affirm, and briefing closed Sept. 4, 2026. No decision was found as of Oct. 8, 2026. A separate primary challenge by Ken McFeeters was dismissed by the state GOP committee on June 14, 2026. To rebut that challenge, his lawyers filed seven years of redacted Alabama income-tax returns (June 1, 2026); the Alabama Department of Revenue declined a records request to confirm his state filing status.

checks.legal: CourtListener and efile/eFD domains were blocked by this environment's proxy, so federal dockets were not searched directly. Searched news archives (AP, APR, Alabama Reflector, ADN, Lagniappe, CNBC, Wikipedia) for civil/criminal cases, Senate Ethics matters and STOCK Act complaints. Found: the 2012–2013 TS Capital investor suit (settled), the 2021 STOCK Act late filings and CLC complaint to Senate Ethics (no public outcome found), and the 2026 residency quo warranto case (pending appeal). Alacourt is paywalled and was not searched.
checks.foreign: FARA (efile.fara.gov) was blocked and not searched. News and the 2020 Senate disclosure (secondary copy) show no foreign-government or foreign-business ties. The only foreign item found was trading in a China-based company's securities (Alibaba options, 2021).
checks.claims: Fixed sample: the campaign site coachforgovernor.com (bio and issues pages) could not be opened (proxy block). Bio claims came from his launch speech and Senate bio. Campaign claims came from his three most-covered 2026 TV ads ('Less taxes, more results', the 'Smarter Plan' school-choice ad, the National Guard crime ad) and his campaign's PAC-money statement. Ad spending is unknown; ADImpact reported about $11,000 digital for the school-choice ad. UPDATE 2026-10-08: coachforgovernor.com still blocked (direct fetch refused; web.archive.org copy blocked). As a stand-in for the campaign bio page, rated the checkable facts on his own Senate 'About Coach' page (4 bio claims). The data-center ad of Oct. 6, 2026 (1819 News) was not added because the sample already uses the most-covered ads.
checks.democracy: NPR/GPB list of Jan. 6–7, 2021 objectors; PBS/AP; Senate Democrats floor record; AP Nov. 2020; Scripps Dec. 2020; Mediaite 2024 and 2026; Wikipedia. senate.gov roll-call pages could not be fetched. Re-checked 2026-10-08: NPR list via GPB lists him among the 6 senators sustaining the Arizona objection (93–6) and the 7 supporting the Pennsylvania objection. The Senate Democrats floor page confirms the 6–93 Arizona tally but does not list names. Official senate.gov roll-call pages were still unreachable, so the item stays 'news'.

legal.t: Seven investors sued him, partner John David Stroud and their TS Capital entities in federal court in February 2012 (an eighth joined later), alleging securities fraud. Stroud pleaded guilty to criminal securities fraud and got 10 years. Tuberville was never charged (investigators said he was also a victim) and settled with the plaintiffs under sealed terms on Oct. 8, 2013.

Reported about 130 stock and option trades from Jan.–May 2021 (worth $894,000 to $3.5 million) after the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline. His office said he was unaware of the trades, filed the report, and paid the late-filing penalty. The Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the Senate Ethics Committee on July 29, 2021.
legal.status: Late-filing penalty paid; no public Senate Ethics action found

research_notes: NOMINEE/BALLOT: Nomination confirmed (May 19, 2026 primary, 85.4%). No independent or third-party governor candidate found in three listings, but the Secretary of State's certified general-election list was not retrieved; a human should confirm on sos.alabama.gov. MONEY (state): fcpa.alabamavotes.gov was blocked by the proxy, so every gubernatorial figure comes from news reports of FCPA filings. Receipts ($15.67M raised since joining the race), disbursements ($9.26M) and COH ($6.56M) through Sept. 30, 2026 are from ADN (Oct. 6, 2026); the Reflector reports $1.13M raised, $4M spent and $6.5M COH for September. Wikipedia's FCPA table shows $14,534,352 raised and $5,167,798 COH as of Aug. 31, but the Reflector reports $9.5M COH at the end of August. These conflict; use ADN/Reflector and check directly on FCPA. Monthly figures: 'May-25' is the campaign's own first-24-hours figure ($2,064,723); Aug-25 is 'just under $700,000' entered as 700,000. Reported PAC money is too partial to compute a PAC share, so src is omitted. Top donors are single reported contributions, not cumulative totals; cumulative top-donor totals need an FCPA pull. No outside (independent) spending in the governor's race was found. MONEY (federal): FEC committee pages read directly for 2019–20, 2021–22, 2023–24 and 2025–26. The 2023–24 individual total, 1,847,627.76, adds FEC's itemized $1,163,376.71 and unitemized $684,251.05. The 2025–26 Senate committee shows $157,000 refunded to other committees and $305,420 to individuals, consistent with winding down his Senate re-election effort; the reason was not documented. COACH PAC (C00762260, his leadership PAC) and Tuberville Victory Fund were not fully reviewed (FEC rate-limited). Club for Growth Action's 2020 spending ($1,433,763) comes from Club for Growth's own release; its donors were not retrieved. Business vs. ideological PAC split not computed. DISCLOSURES: efdsearch.senate.gov was blocked. The eFD index came from a printout hosted on the Jones campaign site (a partisan host of primary records). Use it only as a pointer and verify on eFD. Net worth was not computed. No Alabama Ethics Commission statement of economic interests for 2026 was found or reachable. Lagniappe reported (June 2026) that he released redacted Alabama tax returns for seven years as residency exhibits, and that ALDOR refused to confirm his state filing status. TRADES: count of 1,356 comes from Quiver Quantitative via WBRC (Oct. 2025), not from eFD. The 2021 late filings are the documented STOCK Act violation. No later late-filing violations were confirmed from primary records. VOTES: per instructions, Senate key votes are pulled separately, so israel.votes is left empty for that researcher to fill (e.g., S.J.Res. 111, H.R. 23 cloture, S.Res. 852). The Jan. 6–7, 2021 votes come from NPR's list (via GPB) and PBS/AP because senate.gov could not be fetched. EFFECTIVENESS: congress.gov, GovTrack and Center for Effective Lawmaking pages were blocked or failed, so bills sponsored and CEL scores are omitted and law=3 rests on his office's releases. missed_pct omitted: third-party figures conflict (PolicySoup 7% 'Not Voting' of 915; TheLobbyNews 4.0%, period unstated) and GovTrack was unreachable. FEC RFAI/notices could not be checked (JS-rendered), so recordx.fec is omitted. CLAIMS: coachforgovernor.com was unreachable, so the bio/issues-page part of the mechanical sample could not be run; claims came from ads and statements covered in news (8 claims, 7 checkable). RESIDENCY: the Alabama Supreme Court appeal (Dorgan & LeBlanc v. Tuberville) was fully briefed Sept. 4, 2026, and no ruling was found as of Oct. 8. Re-check before publication. OTHER: the Tommy Tuberville Foundation spent $51,658 of $289,599 raised (about 18%) on charitable causes in 2014–2018, per APR's review of tax filings. AP/NYT reported 'one-third or less.' His campaign disputed this, citing unrecorded donated labor. This is not a legal finding, so it is not under 'legal'. The 2023 military-promotion hold (about 445 nominations, protesting a DoD abortion-travel policy; most released Dec. 5, 2023, the rest ended Dec. 19, 2023) is recorded in Wikipedia and the Reed statement; add it to the votes/record narrative if needed. Photo not added: the Wikimedia file name could not be retrieved. | 2026-10-08 claims pass: added 4 bio claims from his Senate 'About Coach' page (the campaign site was unreachable): SEC titles (true), 2004 Coach of the Year (true), '11 years' at Auburn (partly, since it was 10 seasons), retired 2016 then ESPN (true). The records rest on Wikipedia alone; a human should confirm against Auburn/NCAA record books. Checkable-verdict claims now number 7. Checklist unchanged: democracy stays 'news' because senate.gov roll calls were unreachable; disclosures and ethics stay 'news' and no new eFD or Ethics Commission items were found; the web-search budget was exhausted.

foundation.t: Tommy Tuberville Foundation (founded 2014) raised $289,599 and spent $51,658 (about 18%) on charitable causes in 2014–2018, per APR's review of tax filings; his campaign cited unrecorded donated labor and speaking fees.

military_holds.t: Blocked about 445 senior military promotions for most of 2023 to protest a Pentagon abortion-travel policy. He dropped most holds Dec. 5, 2023, kept holds on four-star officers, and ended them Dec. 19, 2023.
